Much like the British Army’s W10, the Type 20 and 21 are military specifications rather than specific models. These watches were produced by several leading French manufacturers of the time, including Dodane, Airain, Auricoste, Vixa, and Mathey-Tissot. The most famous maker is undoubtedly Breguet, whose Type 20 remains a flagship model today—original examples often fetch tens of thousands. The present example is a Type 21 by Chronofixe, a military supplier/retailer whose watches were manufactured by Mathey-Tissot. And we must say, this is one of the most beautiful, balanced, and visually pleasing chronographs we’ve ever handled. The 38 mm case is unpolished, proudly showcasing its original bevels and sharp edges. The full radium dial and syringe hands are pristine, with all lume intact and now exhibiting a rich pumpkin patina. The two-register layout is clean, functional, and superbly legible. To complete the package, the watch retains its very rare “navigation” bezel (visible in the final images). We’ve recently serviced the watch, and it's running perfectly at +4 s/d, 320 amplitude, with a 0.4 ms beat error

4849fd27d34f: THE ESSENTIALS MAKE: HEUER AUTAVIA MODEL: 2446C YEAR: 1971 BOX/PAPERS: NO/NO CASE DIAMETER: 40mm CASE MATERIAL: STAINLESS STEEL BRACELET MATERIAL: CORFAM MOVEMENT: MANUAL WIND Heuer first applied the name Autavia (a portmanteau of Automotive and Aviation ) back in the 1930s when they produced dash clocks for racing cars and aircraft, signifying its intended use in both automobiles and airplanes. This golden era of motorsport and aviation is still the period most closely associated with the Autavia name. The Heuer Autavia GMT combines Heuer’s mastery of the racing chronograph with a GMT function. The 2446C Mark 4 GMT offered here is in fantastic condition: the dial is clean, all tritium markers are intact and beautifully aged, and the bezel has retained most its original blue and red colours. There are some marks on the white subdials. The MK4 2446 is easily recognisable with its larger subdials, "SWISS" only signature, and red chronograph hand, giving it a different aesthetic to the earlier executions. The pushers are the fluted type, which succeeded the earlier rounded style, and the caseback is the compressor-style snap back. The Valjoux 72 not only looks fantastic but performs superbly, keeping time well. For us, the 2446C is one of the brand’s finest—seldom seen in the wild, deserving of a place in any serious watch collection, and more than capable of holding its own against far more expensive pieces.

Unlike the Milsub—which was essentially an altered 5513—the Sea-Dweller was created because the state-of-the-art dive watch Rolex offered simply wasn’t up to the demands of the rapidly evolving subsea landscape. The reference 1665 was produced from 1967 to 1983 (though it was only sold to civilians from around 1971). Until 1977, these watches were affectionately known as “Double Red Sea-Dwellers” thanks to the two lines of red text. From 1977 to 1983, five further dial variations appeared (Mk0–Mk4), with the Sea-Dweller name and depth rating now printed in white—earning the nickname “Great White.” The present example features a Mk1 dial, seen from around the 5.1m to early 6m serial ranges. Although there is overlap with Mk2 and Mk3 examples, Mk1s are, in our experience, significantly rarer. In fact, we’ve encountered fewer Mk1 Great Whites than DRSDs. Having spent its entire life on the Scottish coast, this watch remains in fantastic condition. The case has been polished before, but likely no more than once or twice. The dial is perfect, with the lume on the markers and hands aged to an even, creamy hue. The original silver date wheel is present. The insert has faded beautifully to a grey–lavender tone. 33beb8feb442: The Rolex Turn-O-Graph is easily one of, if not the most underrated model in the brands history. Predating the — yes, we're going to say it — iconic Submariner by mere months, the Turn-O-Graph Ref. 6202 was in fact the first piece to utilize an externally affixed rotating timing bezel. Early advertisements refer to it as the "simplest 'stop-watch' ever yet waterproof and self-winding!" and depict it being used as a timer for cooking, auto racing, sailing, and even to time phone calls. 094c02582c63: Parisian manufacturer Breguet, named after its founder, Abraham-Louis Breguet, was founded in 1775 and is one of the most stored and historically significant manufacturers in the world of horology. 8f432dcbdea4: Universal Genève was one of the many great brands that succumbed to the quartz crisis of the 1970s. While they disappeared, it was not for their lack of impressive watches. Touted until this very day as an incredible achievement in complicated watchmaking, the ‘Tri-Compax' family of watches was introduced in 1944 and slid in above both the existing chronographs (e.g., Compax, Medico-Compax, Dato-Compax, Film-Compax etc.) as well as the other complicated calendar watches offered by UG at the time as the brands most complicated timepieces. Often viewed as one of watchmaking's great Art Deco dress watches, its origins are far more practical. In fact, the model was conceived not for the drawing room, but for the polo field. During a trip to India in the late 1920s, Swiss businessman César de Trey encountered a British polo player frustrated after cracking the crystal of his watch during a match. The problem lingered with de Trey long after he returned to Switzerland, eventually leading to a discussion with Jacques-David LeCoultre that posed a simple question: what if a watch case could be turned around to protect itself? The solution was as elegant as it was ingenious. By allowing the case to slide and reverse within its carrier, the vulnerable dial and crystal could be hidden away behind a solid metal back whenever play began. For polo players, it meant no more shattered crystals or damaged dials from the inevitable knocks and impacts endured during gameplay. Designed with professional racecar drivers in mind, the Daytona’s precision chronograph and tachymeter bezel allowed drivers to accurately measure speeds up to 400 kilometers or miles per hour. The release of the Daytona came just after Rolex had become the official timekeeper of the Daytona racetrack and the name evolved as a way for the brand to highlight its connection to the celebrated race. Early Daytona models featured a manual-wind Valjoux 72-based column-wheel chronograph movement. This was in use until 1988 when Rolex released the ref. 16520 with an automatic “self-winding” movement. Rolex outsourced this moment, utilizing the Zenith 400 movement, originally manufactured for the “Zenith El-Primero.” For use in the ref. 16520, Rolex required approximately 200 modifications to the Zenith movement, which remained in use for twelve years. fdd9cdc2322c: The Super Compressor case was developed by Ervin Piquerez S.A. (EPSA) in the late 1950s with production lasting into the 1970s. The term "Super Compressor" comes from a Patented design that Ervin Piquerez S.A. The design is complex yet simple in that the deeper in-depth that the watch wen the more watertight the watch would become as a result. The increased pressure by design would allow the case-back to press against the O-ring gasket within the mid-case again increasing water resistance. Super compressors leverage two crowns, one in which operates the winding and setting of the watch and one that operates an inner rotating bezel ring which is also a unique design feature specific to super compressors that allowed for greater security of setting the inner timing bezel inside of the watch instead of externally whereas if the bezel was located externally it could be bumped out of position rendering an accurate measurement of elapsed time. Brands that utilized the super compressor cases included Longines, Hamilton, Universal Genéve, and Enicar. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. T akes on classics such as the Tank and Santos Dumont were followed by new designs, including pieces like the Ellipse, the Tonneau, the Ceinture, and more. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. e173134136c6: The coin watch is a fascinating niche area of horology. cef837e48985: Cartier is a brand that has forever been associated with Opulence, class and sophistication. The company was founded by Louis-François Cartier in 1847 as an ‘ Atelier de Haute Joaillerie ’ after he took over the workshop of his Master, Adolphe Picard. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. T akes on classics such as the Tank and Santos Dumont were followed by new designs, including pieces like the Ellipse, the Tonneau, the Ceinture, and more. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. 9daa6608f12e: The Speedmaster Reference 2998 was the second generation of OMEGA Speedmaster. Launched in 1959 with the 2998-1; the famous ‘Broad Arrow’ hands of the original reference 2915 Speedmasters were replaced by the far narrower ‘Alpha’ hands to aid legibility. This coupled with the exclusive use of a black printed, external tachymeter scale (initially BASE 1000 but changed to BASE 500 in later models) further enhanced its legibility and cemented the Speedmaster as a world class tool watch. It was to become the first OMEGA in space, as Astronaut Walter ‘Wally’ Schirra would take his own personal 2998-4 On board of the Sigma 7, during the Mercury-Atlas 8 mission (October 1962.) The 2998 is an unusual reference as there are 8 different sub-references produced within a space of only 3 years. The Speedmaster was undergoing constant updates with elements of its design and iconography as well as reference nomenclature being modernised throughout its early production. This has led to each sub-reference having its own particular features which were often updated throughout routine servicing making many watches an assembly of various service replacement parts. This makes finding original, correct examples a challenge to locate and has led the 2998 to become a favourite among collectors. e8ea2089ef1f: The founding of Patek Philippe in 1839 can be traced back to the Polish insurrection of 1830. Taking part in the revolt against Russian rule was a young cavalry officer, Antoine Norbert de Patek who, like many of his compatriots was forced to flee Poland and eventually settle in Geneva. Straight away becoming involved in the city’s watchmaking industry, Patek Czapek & Co was founded with a fellow Pole, François Czapek in 1839. Then in 1844 Patek met the French watchmaker, Adrien Philippe in Paris where the latter presented his pioneering keyless winding and setting mechanism. Czapek decided to leave the company in 1845 and Adrien Philippe replaced Czapek as Patek’s partner. The company then changed its name to Patek & Cie before changing once more in 1851 to Patek Philippe & Cie. In 1932, the company was purchased by two brothers Charles and Jean Stern and since then, Patek Philippe S.A. remains a family-owned firm, with the 4th generation at its head. Today, vintage Patek Philippe is a titan in the vintage luxury watch community. Their obsessive attention to detail combined with ground-breaking feats such as the first serially produced, perpetual calendar wristwatches as well as the first split-second chronograph wristwatch, have made Patek Philippe wristwatches and pocket watches some of the most sought after in the world. a0d4841f389a: Cartier is a brand that has forever been associated with Opulence, class and sophistication. The company was founded by Louis-François Cartier in 1847 as an ‘ Atelier de Haute Joaillerie ’ after he took over the workshop of his Master, Adolphe Picard. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. The company was founded by Louis-François Cartier in 1847 as an ‘ Atelier de Haute Joaillerie ’ after he took over the workshop of his Master, Adolphe Picard. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. b6f2de853c3f: The Portugieser exists because someone asked IWC to do the impossible. In the late 1930s, two clients from Portugal approached IWC Schaffhausen with a challenge: build a wristwatch with the accuracy of a marine chronometer. At the time, that meant one thing—scale. IWC’s solution was to house a pocket-watch movement inside a wristwatch case, creating something radically oversized for its time. When the original debuted in 1939, its proportions were shocking, its clarity unmatched. It didn’t follow the rules—it quietly rewrote them. Fast forward to 2015, and the Reference 5102 arrives as a 75th anniversary tribute to that original idea. At 43mm, it remains faithful to the Portugieser’s defining trait: presence with purpose. But what keeps it from feeling oversized is the balance—the wide, open dial, the slim bezel, the long, elegant lugs. The graphic black dial is particularly striking. Printed 'Arabic' numerals anchor the design, while a subsidiary seconds at 6 o’clock reinforces the symmetry. Flip it over, and the real story reveals itself: the hand-wound Caliber 59215, visible through an exhibition caseback, delivering a remarkable 8-day power reserve. It’s mechanical watchmaking at its most satisfying—wind it once, and let it breathe for the better part of a week. Limited to just 750 pieces in stainless steel, this is a Portugieser that feels both reverent and modern—true to its origins, but entirely at ease today. 4da34244b806: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could be completely flipped over? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the caseback with engravings or even miniature portraits. d2de76b5c647: The annual calendar is one of those quietly brilliant complications — the kind that reveals its genius the longer you live with it. 02d1d35c9f8b: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. 7d53791741d7: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. 201ff9438434: For most of its existence, Piaget has operated quietly behind the proverbial horological curtain, producing some of the most impressively thin mechanical movements in Switzerland and supplying them to numerous other maisons . 0cf3ba424576: With a deep connection to motorsport that dates back to the Mille Miglia, it was only natural that Chopard was chosen as a sponsor and official timekeeper for the growing event. There’s no question that cars and watches go together. And when they come together in watch form, man, do we love it, and we’re sure you will too.
2abedc469a11: Seiko's Tuna dive watches are known by the nicknames of "Baby Tuna," "Golden Tuna" and "Grandfather Tuna," but they could also be known as "big," "bigger," and "biggest." But rather than being big simply for the sake of it, the size of the Tunas has functionality at its heart. Seiko had released its first dive watch in 1965, the Reference 6217 (or 62-MAS). The 62-MAS was water-resistant to 150 meters and had a rotating bezel, luminous hour markers, and a 17-jewel movement (Calibre 6127) with a beat rate of 18,000. It was an excellent effort, competitively-priced compared to Swiss divers, but for Seiko, it was only the beginning. In 1968, a letter from a disgruntled professional diver in Hiroshima led to a seven year odyssey that resulted in the creation of the Tuna series of dive watches, the first ever designed specifically for saturation diving. A team of engineers led by Ikuo Tokunaga devised a circular, titanium one-piece or monocoque case with a special "L type" gasket, surrounded by a titanium shroud coated with ceramic. The crystal was held in place with a locking ring. This eliminated the need for a Helium Escape Valve, resulting in a watch that--released in 1975-looked entirely different from any dive watch that had been released. The Reference 6159-7010 was the first in a lineage of "Tuna" divers with hockeypuck aesthetics built for one purpose: never to fail. Packing 600M of water resistance, the overbuilt dive masterpiece inspired the full lineage of Tuna models w
db6eeb486982: We. Love. Polerouters. Most likely, this will come as no great shock to those of you who know us. 67d5f3c915c1: In 1960, Bulova had a vision of the future — and that future hummed with potential! About a decade before the Quartz Crisis, Bulova introduced a watch that did away with the traditional balance wheel, instead using a 360-hertz tuning fork attached to a battery-powered transistor oscillator circuit as its heart. Designed by Max Hetzel, the Accutron made waves, becoming the first wristwatch precise enough to be qualified for U.S. Railroad certification — guaranteed to be accurate to about one minute per month, or roughly two seconds per day. Originally designed to be a salesman's tool highlighting the inner mechanism of the Accutron movement, the Spaceview wasn't intended for retail purchase. But the delight of seeing these inner workings displayed caused demand from retailers and consumers to spike; indeed, seemingly everyone wanted this open-worked watch to wear and take home. Bulova responded, producing retail versions with the same unique characteristics of their display models. The Accutron Spaceview was unlike anything that came before, and really, anything since. In production for about 17 years, the tuning fork technology was eventually beaten out by quartz crystal movements, making these watches relatively short-lived. But they contain important and revolutionary technology that has had a tremendous impact on today's world. 70bf0cb04f44: When we think of watches from the 1970's, one thing comes to mind: Funky case shapes! Thriving in the 1960s-1970s, the American company had a seemingly endless catalog of funky sports watches, particularly in the dive and chronograph categories. Divers featuring a "666 Feet" depth reading on the dial have colloquially become known as 'Devil Divers' and have developed a cult following. This particular piece, an Oceanographer Devil Diver, dates to circa 1970s and features a 41mm stainless steel cushion case with an acrylic crystal, a signed crown, a screw-down caseback, a red and black dive bezel, a matte black crosshair Tritium dial with applied 'crystal' indices, and an automatic movement within. With all of these fine details, features, and designs, it is easy to see why these 'Devil Divers' are quickly developing a cult following. a8ade13bc8a5: If you think Zodiac is all dive watches and military grit, think again. Founded in 1882 in Le Locle, Zodiac earned its place in history with serious tool watches like the Sea Wolf — one of the earliest commercially available dive watches, worn by soldiers and adventurers alike. But just as important is the brand’s willingness to get a little strange. By the late 1960s and into the ’70s, Zodiac was pushing design into far more experimental territory, creating watches that felt less like instruments and more like ideas. The Orbiter Automatic sits squarely in that world. Housed in a gold-plated case, it features one of Zodiac’s signature “mystery” dial layouts — a display that feels almost futuristic even today. There’s no conventional seconds hand here; instead, a red dot orbits the dial, tracing time in a hypnotic loop. Hours and minutes are indicated by floating markers that appear detached from any central pinion, giving the entire display a sense of weightlessness. Paired with a Zodiac-signed, NSA-manufactured mesh bracelet, the watch wears exactly as it should: fluid, comfortable, and unmistakably of its era. Playful, unconventional, and just a little bit mind-bending, this is Zodiac at its most creative — a reminder that sometimes the best-designed watches don’t just tell time, they reinterpret it.
7e81ea5d149b: In an era defined by exploration — of oceans, skies, and the most remote corners of the globe — watchmakers were tasked with building instruments that could keep up. 19c5ae216ff9: Modern dive watches tend to fall into one of two camps: those that trade on nostalgia, and those that genuinely push the category forward. The Tudor Pelagos M25600TB-0001 is firmly in the latter. While its design nods to the brand’s historic tool watches, the Pelagos was conceived from the ground up as a contemporary instrument — one that prioritizes function, durability, and thoughtful engineering over sentimentality. Executed entirely in titanium, the 42mm case is both lightweight and exceptionally robust, outfitted with a helium escape valve and rated to a formidable 500 meters of water resistance. Fitted with Tudor’s spring-loaded, self-adjusting clasp, it automatically compensates for changes in wrist size — whether from temperature shifts or a wetsuit compressing at depth. It’s an elegant solution to a real-world problem, and one that underscores the watch’s no-nonsense approach to utility. 03fea9f993d6: There are tourbillons that announce themselves — and then there are those, like this A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Tourbillon ref. 730.079F , that quietly assert their authority. Introduced as part of Lange’s most classically minded family, the 1815 Tourbillon is already a study in restraint, but this enamel-dial variant elevates that ethos to something approaching purity. cea44a85a75e: There are jewelry watches. And then there are small, subversive sculptures that happen to tell time. This 1960s Omega watch belongs firmly in the latter category. Its elaborate 18K yellow-gold bracelet explodes across the wrist in a nugget-meets-lava formation. An organic, 'coral-like' lattice that feels less fabricated than unearthed. Created during one of Omega’s most adventurous design periods, the piece throws polite Swiss restraint out the window. The result is a watch that behaves more like a sculpture than timekeeper, a small eruption of gold across the wrist where form, texture, and imagination take the lead. The petite champagne dial—complete with slender 'baton' indices and 'sword' hands—has a truly elegant presence in a sea of gold. It’s intimacy by design. The crown is tucked discreetly on the caseback, preserving the uninterrupted sculptural silhouette. Inside beats a manual-wind Omega Calibre , a slim, reliable movement suited perfectly to refined ladies’ watches of the era. Omega has long understood that women’s watches can be mechanically serious and aesthetically daring. This piece proves it. Part avant-garde jewel, part timekeeping instrument, fully wearable art. A wildly confident design period in Omega’s history. One that deserves far more attention than it gets.
ba2f3b6e6cb1: Breguet’s timepieces are more than simple wristwatches — they’re works of art. This example, a Reference 7027, is a drop-dead gorgeous melding of classic Breguet aesthetics that grabs your attention and doesn't let go. 504950e00109: The ‘Paul Newman’ Daytona — in all its various guises — is one of the most desirable watches in the world. 5017167390b3: In 1996, Patek Philippe made one of its most brilliant strategic moves— the introduction and development of the Annual Calendar complication. Patek recognized a gap in offerings between the simple and (relatively) accessible Calatrava classic dress watches and the complicated, and in turn, highly expensive, Grand Complications. The so-called "Annual Calendar" bridged the gap between these two price points, offering a natural progression for collectors looking to access a Patek complication at a more accessible price point. The Annual Calendar needs adjusting just once per year. This change enables the movement to be far more economical to produce, easier to service, and more affordable to purchase. The inaugural Reference 5035 Annual Calendar of 1996 was a tremendous success, and ever since, Patek's Annual Calendars have been a popular favorite. Annual Calendars from Patek represent the bread and butter of the brand— perfectly executed, complicated dress watches. In 2006, Patek Philippe introduced the Reference 5960P, a platinum annual calendar featuring a flyback chronograph. Distinguished from the other annual calendars because of its decidedly sporty look, the 5960 stood out from the crowd. It wasn't only noteworthy for the flyback; however, it also featured a modern annual calendar layout. d8887459ba1a: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6119G-001, builds on the foundational designs of its three-hand predecessors and is housed in a 39mm white gold case with a guilloché Clous de Paris bezel, signed crown, a sapphire crystal and a svelte case profile that will delight any wrist. The dial features a dynamic, vertically satin brushed anthracite tone acting as a canvas for its applied gold indices, the constant-seconds subsidiary register at 6 o’clock, a 'dauphine' handset and a white-accented ‘railroad’ minute track Powered and visible by way of a sapphire exhibition caseback, this Calatrava features a hand-wound Patek Philippe Calibre 30-255 PS and comes fitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with a signed 18K white gold pin
f05800904f94: Oftentimes in the hobby of watch collecting, there can be a bit too much focus on what the hot watch of the moment might be - the piece that no one can get, or the watch that everyone wants to own purely so they can say they own it. But in this frenzy of emphasis on what the next big windfall investment piece might be, there are literally tons of watches and brands which slip woefully under the radar. Tissot is among those brands. This particular Tissot is a modern beauty unlike anything else in the price category. A manually-wound skeleton, this piece has no real dial, with a complete openwork look into the industrial movement design architecture. The midcase is brushed, with a brushed bezel and polished case band. It's particularly exciting to see brands like Tissot investing in manually-wound movements. For a modernist look into traditional watchmaking, you'd be hard pressed to beat this piece at the price point! This one will go fast!
53bf6e8d2af0: Patek Philippe may be known for its complicated calendar watches, but it’s equally renowned for the simple, elegant dress watches it makes for both men and women. Once you take it for a spin, you're sure to be as smitten with its charms as we are!

However, some were more innovative than others. Take this exquisite piece from Piaget, specialists in ultra-thin watchmaking: seamlessly machined such that there’s no perceivable break from watch head to bracelet, it’s as much akin to a piece of jewelry as it is to a more traditional wristwatch. Housed in a 34mm, yellow gold and white gold two tone alternating case with a fantastic, integrated bracelet with a signed clasp, this Polo features a two tone dial with brushed yellow gold components and bands of white gold diamond-set striping. With its eye-catching design, fascinating dial, and awesome bracelet, this is a standout timepiece appropriate for virtually any wrist. This piece could easily be mistaken for a bracelet with the design carrying straight onto the dial. That’s really part of the charm of so many of Piaget’s late 20th century watch designs. While these pieces went underappreciated for many years, we have recently seen
4b65c5f551b3: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, comes in with a 30mm stainless steel reversible case featuring an exhibition caseback on the reverse side. The front facing dial features a classic 'Arabic' layout with subsidiary seconds and a guilloche di
cc19b0539fa9: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, and the original Breitling Chronomat models of 1942 were built from the ground up to be no-nonsense instruments for use in the cockpit. Its matte black dial conveys a plethora of information: An outer tachymeter scale and 1/5th-seconds track are joined by an outsized date window between 4 and 5 o'clock, applied luminous indices, and a triple-register chronograph display with running seconds, 12-hour, and 30-minute registers. A luminous 'sword' handset rounds out the feature set. Powered by the automatic Breitling B01 chronograph movement with a 70 hour power reserve, this hardy tool watch comes paired to its correct stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed folding clasp. Happily, it also includes its kit. In need of a serious everyday tool watch that you don't have to baby? Look no further!
f95d24230016: You might know Montblanc as a pen-maker, but that’s not the entire story. World famous for its writing instruments and leather goods, Montblanc began making watches in 1997. 72db9bdcb1d8: Just one look at the variety of multi-timezone watches available on the market (and across the price spectrum!) can make your head spin. Dynamic in all types of lighting, it features applied indices with polished luminous surrounds, a fully graduated rehaut , an AM/PM indicator at 9 o’clock, a recessed subsidiary date dial and a luminous ‘stick’ handset accompanied by an additional arrow hour hand to keep track of local time — which by the way features a a nifty function that allows it to sneak in under the main hour hand to keep the dial neat and tidy while you enjoy being grounded at home. e9b3b76bc747: The Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and has in recent years once again become one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. ed7bcae80524: Tudor’s legacy as maker of high-quality tool watches was cemented long before the brand re-entered the American market in late 2013. Back in the 1990s and early 2000s, the brand was calling upon its legacy products to inspire a fresh crop of tool watches to satisfy the modern collector. This Tudor Prince Date chronograph Ref. 79280 all of those boxes: Housed in a 40mm stainless steel Oyster case with screw-down chronograph pushers, a signed crown, a sapphire crystal, and a steel tachymeter bezel insert, it features a black dial with an outer 1/5th-seconds track, a triple-register chronograph display in black and white, a magnified date window at 3 o'clock, and a luminous 'baton' handset with a central chrono seconds. 345961d44485: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, but in the 1950's, the budding popularity of dive watches such as the Rolex Submariner and the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms pushed it to enter that race. In 1957, the brand released both a time-only dive watch, the Superocean Reference 1004, and a chronograph in the form of the Reference 807. 0a42779f7cd0: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. Since then, numerous Breitling chronographs have seen action in myriad scenarios, not the least of which is on the wrists of athletes and ordinary folks simply going about their business, who need a strong, reliable watch to time everyday events. The Breitling Endurance Pro in particular stands out for its versatile use cases, being equally at home out in the field or simply out for a stroll. Housed in a 44mm polymer Breighlight case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, 'piston' pushers, and a black polymer, bi-directional 'compass' bezel, it features a luminous red fume dial with applied 'Arabic' indices, a matching handset, a triple-register chronograph with a date window at 4:30, and an inner pulsometer scale around the dial periphery. 300a807148eb: From the 1920s through the 1940s, small ladies’ cocktail watches were all the rage. These delicate timepieces — thin, often crafted in precious metals and paired with integrated bracelets — were designed as much as jewelry as they were instruments for telling time. With their diminutive dials and finely crafted movements, they offered elegance without excess, making them the perfect companions for evenings out and formal occasions. This particular example, retailed by Tiffany & Co., captures that spirit beautifully. The petite, round platinum case is richly set with diamonds, extending seamlessly into a refined, 'tennis-style' bracelet that wraps the wrist in light. The design feels distinctly mid-century, with subtle Art Deco undertones in its symmetry and geometry, yet remains effortlessly wearable today. The dial provides a quiet counterpoint to the brilliance surrounding it. Softly patinated and restrained, it features 'Arabic' numerals, a delicate minute track, and slender 'Breguet-style' hands that keep the focus on clarity and proportion. It’s a thoughtful balance, with just enough detail to ground the watch without competing with the case's sparkle. Light, graceful, and unapologetically elegant, it reflects a time when watches were designed to accompany candlelight, champagne, and the understated glamour of an evening out on the town.
8836045822e5: The Portugieser was so-called because two IWC clients from Portugal approached the manufacture with a somewhat daunting task: to produce a wristwatch that was just as accurate as a marine chronometer. In those days, the only way to ensure that degree of accuracy in a wristwatch would be to cannibalize a movement from a pocket watch and put it in a wristwatch case. The watches the resulted from such a union were large, a huge departure from the slim cases that typified wristwatches of the era. So that’s what IWC did, using a Hunter Calibre 74 pocket watch movement to create the first Portugieser. In 2015, IWC released the watch that we have here, the Reference 5102 Portuguieser made to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the original Portuguieser which debuted in 1939. This watch comes in at the same size as the original too, at 43mm wide. At the time, the standard size of most men's watches was closer to 33mm or 34mm, so while this watch isn't exactly small now, it would have been absolutely massive 75 years ago! This watch features a gorgeous matte black dial with printed 'Arabic' quadrant numerals, a subsidiary seconds counter at the 6:00 position, and an exhibition caseback, displaying the IWC Calibre 59215 hand-cranking movement with a massive 8-day power reserve. With only 750 examples made in steel, this is an excellent opportunity to pick up a contemporary classic with its full kit, and one of IWC's best releases in recent years!
de93c9068174: There’s a particular kind of confidence in doing less, and doing it exceptionally well. Powered by a manual-wind movement, it stays true to traditional watchmaking while maintaining an almost jewelry-like presence. d562593e78eb: There are few names in watchmaking that carry the same quiet authority as Breguet — and even fewer that can claim to have shaped the very language of modern horology. Founded in 1775 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, the maison is responsible for some of the most important inventions in watchmaking history, including the tourbillon, the Breguet overcoil, and the 'pare-chute' shock protection system. Just as influential, however, is the brand’s design vocabulary: engine-turned guilloché dials, elegant 'Roman' numerals, and those unmistakable blued 'Breguet' hands. These weren’t just aesthetic choices — they were innovations in legibility and refinement, developed for an elite clientele that included royalty, scientists, and statesmen. That balance of technical mastery and visual restraint remains at the core of Breguet today. This Ladies’ Classique Ref. 8561 is a perfect expression of that enduring philosophy. Crafted in 18K white gold, the 25.5mm case is elegantly framed by a diamond-set bezel and lugs, adding brilliance without disrupting the watch’s elegance. Blued steel hands sweep across 'Roman' numerals with that unmistakable Breguet grace, while a signed crown, marked with the maison’s “B,” completes the overall design. Powered by a manual-wind movement and paired with a complementary burgundy a
c39d088c64ab: Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, feels that women's sports watches should be just as compelling as men's pieces. e71d5d242b8a: The IWC Pilot's Watch can trace its history back to the oversized timepieces produced for military aviators in 1940. 12a5d263aef8: In the 1950s and 1960s, the cocktail watch wasn’t just an accessory, it was part of the occasion. These pieces were designed to disappear into the rhythm of an evening, catching light rather than attention, pairing effortlessly with silk, champagne, and late hours. 9b721b80c61f: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. Though many storied brands produced notable chronographs during the complication’s heyday from the 1930s through the 1970s, numerous other firms fell by the wayside during the Quartz Crisis, folding completely and disappearing or being rolled up into conglomerates that pillaged their stores of parts. Heuer, for its part, is still around today as TAG Heuer, but its pre-TAG period was perhaps its most fertile era of chronograph design. Take the Calculator watch, for example: this special model took advantage of the brand's esteemed automatic chronograph movement technology and paired it with a unique two-part slide rule bezel in what can best be described as a sort of mechanical calculator: Using the bezel, the wearer can easily calculate distance and weight and convert between metric and imperial. Pretty neat! This particular Heuer Calculator watch, a Reference 110.633, dates to the 1970s and features a 45.5mm 'tonneau-shaped' stainless steel case with an outer calculator bezel, dual 'pump' pushers, a left-hand crown, and a stainless steel multi-link bracelet. Its d
d87b1c90c88f: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. In spite of the unique design, this piece still preserves many of the details of classic Cartier we would hope to see: a 'Roman' numeral dial, blued steel hands, petite Cartier logo, and more all serve as a reminder that this piece is backed by a name with an unrivaled history for fine jewelry making, and yes, watchmaking too. A Baignoire on a leather strap is a solid choice for any occasion. However, a Baignoire on an integrated bracelet is seemingly more our style!
ade061f7ed0d: Seiko makes fantastic watches. Pure and simple. From the rare as hen's teeth Hi-Beat 6159 to the film-famous 6105 and 6309 models to the economy workhorse SXK007, Japanese watchmakers perfected incredibly well-made tool watches decades ago - and at prices that make the most diehard Swiss watch fans question their spending habits. This piece, a Reference SRQ057 , dates to 2025 and recalls one of the coolest pieces of Seiko history. The incredible chrono we have here is a tribute limited edition of the Datsun, sporting the advantages of modern watchmaking including sapphire crystals and an updated automatic movement. The piece measures 42mm in diameter and features an automatic movement within. Built on a reputation for fine chronograph construction, this Seiko is one to save for the ages, recalling one of the coolest moves in Seiko history. These are wonderful timepieces that represent just about everything that we love about Seiko and are overlooked by many. Don't make that mistake!
b7d16caff5e6: The Cartier Tank Americaine is quite possibly the least understood model in Cartier's lineup. Introduced in 1989, it is, in many ways, a modern update to the classic Cintrée. This particular example is a beautiful ladies' Reference W2620031-2503 cased in 18K rose gold, and features the timeless satin silver guilloché dial with printed 'Roman' indices upon which Cartier was built. The silver guilloché dial — fitted with an inner 'railroad' minute track and blued steel 'sword' handset — is a straightforward picture of pure class. Meanwhile, a handy quartz movement and a stunning scale-link bracelet in 18K rose gold with a hidden butterfly clasp seal the deal. The Tank Louis is all well and good. But for our money, this incredible, elongated Americaine is equally deserving of your attention!

add0475d231d: Never underestimate the power of a field-style Movado watch. Especially one from their mid-century output, a period when the brand was quietly producing some of the most thoughtful, well-balanced designs in Swiss watchmaking. Not loud, not flashy, just consistently right. This 1950s Movado Ref. 18126 is a perfect example. Housed in a 34mm stainless steel case with faceted lugs and an acrylic crystal, it strikes that ideal balance between durability and elegance. It wears like a field watch, compact, legible, and practical, but carries the refinement of a proper dress piece. The dial is where it really comes together. A warm champagne tone, aged into a rich, almost salmon hue, gives the watch a sense of depth and character that only time can produce. Applied 'Arabic' numerals and 'diamond' markers keep things highly legible, while the 'syringe' hands add a graphic strength to the dial. At six o’clock, a recessed sub-seconds register anchors the layout, adding symmetry without clutter. Powered by a hand-wound movement, it’s everything you need, nothing you don’t. A versatile vintage piece that feels just as right today as it did the day it left the factory. The kind of watch that doesn’t try to impress, yet ends up doing exactly that!
3ff8e629db72: Early Pilot Chronographs are straight up cool. Regardless of the name on the dial, these watches from the 50s easily catch our attention. In the 1940s, watches made by Benrus were flying off the shelves… literally. And among them, the best-known is this watch: the Sky Chief, perhaps one of the most perfect pilot’s watches ever made. The Sky Chief, introduced in 1940, is without a doubt the brand’s most famous chronograph. Though it was released in several variations (including triple-date models), it’s the pilot’s version that’s become the most iconic. At first glance, it’s a tool watch, looking much like the chronographs worn by the world’s air forces. This Benrus Sky Chief features a heavily patinated three register silver-tone dial with a coin-edged finish to the bezel. The bi-directional rotating bezel features a tiny red timing indicator, a small but important detail that so many of these mid-century chronographs feature. Elongated blued steel hands stretch across the dial as well as fill the sub-dials. This piece represents an important element of the watch industry of the 50s, an industry that endeavored to build capable tools for a purpose. If you're into adding unique vintage chronographs to your collection that don't break the bank, this Benrus might just be the perfect solution.

b12a92129e87: One of the most common requests we get are for affordable vintage super compressors, and it's truly no surprise to us. Super compressor watches, noted for their unique water proofing system and recognizable twin-crown display, these peices have an incredible degree of cool and pack vintage charm to the nines. If you're here, you know we have a particular affection for off-brand timepieces- there are an untold number of fantastic watches that combine sharp looks, robust build quality, and time-tested movements just as well as the bigger names at a fraction of the price. If you've never heard of Royce before, we wouldn't blame you. While the brand dates back to the 1920's, they spent decades turning out simple, reliable watches with high-grade cases and movements before falling victim to the quartz crisis like so many other brands. c8756629f6b7: The Reverso, Jaeger-LeCoultre's most distinctive watch, certainly has an impressive pedigree. One of the world's first sports watches, the Reverso combined utility with a sleek and elegant Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance an Art Deco dress watch, it owes its conception to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the 1920s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea that had taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the impact problem polo players could face on the field. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. 764920d77580: Few names in Swiss watchmaking carry the quiet authority of Girard-Perregaux. This automatic winding dress watch is an excellent example of what we mean. In the 1950s, the newest developments in watch technology revolved around automatic winding movement development, and GP was at the forefront. 9de6558ea490: When it comes to vintage dive watches, we love the heavy hitters just as much as the next guy. The Certina DS-2 falls into that select group of watches. This brilliantly over-engineered 200 meter diver was made in the 1970s and features a lovely blue dial. 193c567daf63: There are certain designs that resonate throughout the years and remain evergreen despite changing trends and tastes. The Cartier Tank, in all its one hundred-plus years of production, is one such design. 628ea4f7c514: Patek Philippe made a fantastic, stainless steel sports watch — and we're not talking about the Aquanaut or the Nautilus. 5c397693bc0c: Breitling was an early pioneer in the development of precision-made cockpit instruments for pilots. a28f7ad00104: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. 9aa20357e5e3: Collectors of vintage chronographs should know Longines well. Their chronographs of the 1930s and 1940s represent the pinnacle of chronograph production. Upon its release, the 13ZN became a favorite among aviators, who used the feature for navigation, and has gained something of a cult status among modern collectors. But while the 13ZN has certainly gained a respectable following, there are other early chronographs by Longines that deserve consideration--not just because of their rarity. The Longines monopusher or chronostop combines two elements that Longines did well, yet rarely put together: a central-minutes counter and a single pusher. The single or monopusher chronograph is a holdover from the days when watches were carried in the pocket, not worn on the wrist. The origin of the chronograph in pocket watches is disputed, but it's known that master French watchmaker, Louis Moinet, produced a stopwatch-like timepiece in 1816. 8599252843cd: The Jet Age shrunk the world. 9b83d6c59d47: These days, we’re overly reliant on our devices for daily task alerts. In the past, 'alerts' could come in a vastly more engaging mechanical form, such as a mechanical alarm. This Fortis Brain Matic — an incredible name for a watch if ever there was one — is one such alarm watch. 83a9246406f9: Vintage chronographs aren’t just inventory for us — they’re origin stories. bd4484cf37fb: No, it’s not a Tank. And yes, it deserves your attention! d662b1f4892e: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t often get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. dccc48b355a6: The Space Age didn’t just put men on the moon; it reshaped design on Earth. Cars, furniture, architecture… and watches began to take on a certain orbital cool. This 1960s Seiko Chariot “Disco Volante” is a perfect artifact of that moment. The flying saucer silhouette is pure mid-century optimism, capped by a domed acrylic crystal that enhances the watch’s smooth, glowing presence. The hammered bezel is the subtle twist: textured just enough to catch the light, adding dimension to an otherwise clean, architectural case. The silver sunray dial reflects like brushed aluminum under studio lights. Minimal printed indices keep things disciplined, allowing the faceted bezel and sharp handset to do the talking. Even the original “nipple” crown remains crisp — a small but satisfying detail for those who notice. Inside beats Seiko’s manually wound 21-jewel cal. 6660, proof that behind the playful form lies serious mechanical integrity. A simple glowing disk. Steel restraint. Space-age clarity. A reminder that sometimes the coolest move is restraint, resulting in a watch that feels just as modern today as it did the day it debuted.
67b9315ea27b: There’s a particular kind of confidence required to make a watch this restrained. Minimalism, done correctly, never goes out of style.

0ff1993eb292: A secret, squared—and unmistakably Gilbert Albert. A hidden dial by a designer’s designer. Time, disguised as art.

20648ae751ab: Watches have been indispensable tools for explorers since John Harrison created his marine chronometer in the 1760s, even as more sophisticated technologies like radar emerged in the 20th century. But none of this could have happened without John Harrison’s chronometer; before he developed it in the 1760s, successful navigation was more a product of luck than science. The problem wasn’t latitude, but longitude. Navigators could determine their latitude by the angle of the sun at noon, or that of Polaris—the North Star—at twilight. But the rolling motion of a ship at sea rendered that method impossible when it came to determining longitude. Although scientists suggested using an accurate clock—or chronometer—for that purpose as early as the 1500s, early attempts proved insufficient when faced with the endless undulation of the ocean. This problem would prove deadly in 1707, when a fleet of four warships floundered on the rocks surrounding the Isles of Scilly. b4ccdc3c94eb: The 1970s were not a timid decade — and neither is this Tissot. This Seastar Navigator Chronograph captures that era’s confidence in full color. 195ef172781c: The story of Bulova is deeply entwined with American manufacturing. The brand was among the first to offer a wide range of wristwatches for men, with a distinctive visual style that—thanks to its innovative adoption of advertising and a relocation to Astoria, Queens—became fixed in the American imagination. Bulova took over offices in the Empire State Building and installed an observatory on the roof, in order to measure universal time. In the workshop down below, watchmakers timed the watches they were working on to readings taken in the observatory. 687014fec92f: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, a Reference Q2601410, is a beautiful ladies' model. aaf30a68d661: In the early 1970s, the future didn’t tick — it hummed. Powered by the legendary Accutron Caliber 218 (Bulova’s legendary battery-driven tuning fork movement), this isn’t a traditional mechanical watch. There’s no balance wheel oscillating inside. Introduced as the successor to the iconic 214, the 218 series refined the formula. Most notably, it returned the crown to a more conventional position (often at 4 o’clock), making it easier to set and wear in everyday life. The "N6" code indicates the year of production. The "N" signifies the 1970s decade, and the "6" indicates the specific year 1976. And that dial! A lovely 'Holographic' champagne dial with applique indexes complement the two-tone bracelet. It’s pure 1970s optimism, bold, modern, slightly space-age, yet surprisingly wearable today. The case proportions feel architectural, grounded, and substantial without veering into excess. The Accutron line famously found its way onto the wrists of astronauts, pilots, and even into cockpit instrumentation, cementing its reputation as the watch of the electronic age. Bulova responded, producing retail versions with the same unique characteristics of their display models. The Accutron Spaceview was unlike anything that came before, and really, anything since. The whole of the dial has a textured finish to it that contrasts with each of the refined details. 0c7cadcbc803: Long time ago, in a galaxy far far away, Seiko was leaps and bounds ahead of their time. 4a83df8c1f16: While Movado is now best known as a producer of fashion watches like the Museum Watch, Movado's roots go much deeper than that. Incredible. This set up Movado's next trick - the Curviplan. In aesthetics, the Curviplan is somewhat adjacent to the Polyplan. It features a slender silhouette that curves and also features extended bridges. While the calibre remains akin to a traditional movement construction, the Curviplan features the Calibre 510 - a suitable companion to the Polyplan. Nevertheless, on that winter day in 1969, Zenith proudly displayed a working model of its chronograph. The A386 was the first model to be fitted with the El Primero movement, and therefore commands a hefty premium among collectors for its horological import. 5578fa807eac: There are certain designs that just resonate throughout the years and remain evergreen despite changing trends and tastes. The Cartier Tank, in all its one hundred-plus years of production, is one such design. Whether in gold (yellow, pink, or white), stainless steel, or vermeil; whether Française, Chinoise, Americaine, or Normale; the Tank by Cartier is one watch that truly deserves to be called "iconic." Cartier introduced the Tank in 1917, with a run of six pieces — given, or so the legend goes, to American General Joseph Pershing and his staff. The design of the Tank was inspired by the Renault FT-17 tanks Cartier glimpsed on the battlefield of the Great War. (Cartier took the look of the Renault tank's treads and applied it to the lugs, which were integrated via brancards into the case itself.) That first run of six pieces increased to thirty-three by 1920, and by the end of the 20th century, that number stood well in the thousands. In sheer volume alone, the Tank — in all its various models — is Cartier's largest line of watches. The Tank Louis was introduced in 1922, following close on the heels of the Asian-influenced Tank Chinoise. With the Tank Louis, Cartier went back to basics, with the classic lugs that resemble the treads that inspired them. Louis Cartier himself wore the watch that bore his name — that association with the man himself marks the Tank Louis as the quintessence of the Cartier Tanks. Representing one of the first releases from the George Kern-led Breitling era, it’s an important model in Navitimer history, and a fantastic everyday watch from a beloved marque.

Despite the developing dive watch market caused by the emergence of recreational SCUBA diving, IWC seemed resistant to enter the fray. With the Fifty Fathoms’s association with Jacques Cousteau and the Submariner's as-then unsurpassed depth rating of 200m, there seemed little room for improvement in dive watches. ac80c0d7d92f: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t often get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. Of course, this is nonsense — there’s no reason whatsoever that a lady’s watch should be any less considered than a man’s! Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, clearly doesn't feel this way. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design compelling timepieces with unusual designs. This particular Enigma is an exceptional piece fashioned from stainless steel. Encapsulating exactly the type of design-first mentality that Enigma took in crafting its unique pieces, it features a sapphire cabochon crown and a sapphire crystal. This piece most notably boasts an asymmetrical, almost claw-like case profile unlike anything else on the market, plus a handsome guilloche silver dial with applied 'baton' and 'Arabic' indices and a 'dauphine' handset. The blue leather strap integrates directly into the case for a seamless flow tied together by a stainless steel deployant clasp, while a handy quartz movement serves as the power plant. For someone on the hunt for a design-forward timepiece to accompany an elegant night at a soirée or gala, it's an ideal choice. And did we mention it comes with its box and papers?

550c1bfce017: The design language of the 1970s was bold, funky, and colorful. Sporting chronographs from this era are quite unlike anything that came before. Unlike the first series Carreras, the design language of the second generation featured the cushion case popularized by models such as the Autavia and Montreal, and Heuer began fitting their Calibre 11 automatic movements into them in 1969. This example, a Reference 510.523, features a 38mm stainless steel with a black dial set with orange chronograph seconds hand, a three register layout arranged on the left side of the dial, and a date window at 3 o'clock. This cushion-case piece is outfitted with caliber 5100 by Lemania, and dates to the 1980s as a modern extension of the classic Heuer design language. If you are searching for a Heuer that is a bit more funky - and considerably less expensive - than the earliest versions, have a look at this beauty!
654ef52880f9: In 1968, Patek Philippe released the Golden Ellipse. Debuting eight years before the iconic Nautilus, the Ellipse — with its distinctive oval shape — was unlike anything else in Patek Philippe’s catalogs. In period, the Ellipse line became emblematic of the era for design and signaled an elevated level of taste, particularly given the popularity of function-first tool watches that defined the 1960s for many. In the intervening years, the Ellipse and many of its contemporaries fell out of favor with collectors who favored purpose-built steel chronographs and divers that were closely associated with tales of adventure and exploration. a9220fb9cc26: Alfred Lugrin, a highly skilled watchmaker who trained at Jaeger-LeCoultre, founded his workshop in 1884 in Switzerland’s Vallée de Joux — a region long regarded as the heart of traditional Swiss watchmaking. Between 1928 and 1930, the company officially adopted the name "Lemania Watch Co.," inspired by Lac Léman, the French name for Lake Geneva. During the economic hardships of the Great Depression, Lemania joined forces with Omega and Tissot to form the SSIH group (Société Suisse pour l’Industrie Horlogère), a move that helped secure the future of all three brands. Within the group, Lemania became the primary movement supplier to Omega, a partnership that would go on to shape some of the most important chronographs ever produced. Throughout the 1940s and 1950s, Lemania developed a series of legendary calibres, most notably the celebrated CH27 movement, later known at Omega as the Calibre 321. This movement would go on to power the Omega Speedmaster and eventually became the first and only mechanical chronograph movement flight-qualified by NASA for manned space missions. 8e7d54548671: Since its official debut in 1956, the Day-Date has been produced exclusively in precious metals. As the flagship model of the Genevan manufacturer, it has long been synonymous with success, frequently seen on the wrists of heads of state, royalty, and other influential figures. Most Day-Dates were fitted with discreet, conservative dials—after all, most buyers of this model preferred elegance over extravagance. But Rolex made a notable exception to this unwritten rule: beginning in the 1970s, they introduced bright, high-gloss lacquered dials known today as “Stella” dials. At the time, these bold colours were not widely embraced, precisely because they attracted attention. As a result, production numbers remained low, making them highly sought after today. A wide array of colours is known—yellow, green, orange, red ,pink and multiple shades of blue, some embellished with gemstones, and produced across different metals. They also span various generations: from the early 18xx “pie-pan” versions to the later 18xxx models with flat dials. The manufacturing process was exceptionally labor-intensive. Each dial was spray-painted and then oven-baked to set the pigment. This cycle was repeated multiple times until the desired depth of colour and finish was achieved. Afterward, the dial was polished and coated with a clear lacquer. This final step created the distinctive effect where the printed text appears to float above the glossy surface, reminiscent of the porcelain-dial Daytonas.

c6ffd2ecd2f6: The story of the Patek Philippe World Time complication begins with Louis Cottier, a Geneva watchmaker who invented the modern world time mechanism in the early 1930s. His system allowed the wearer to read the time in 24 time zones simultaneously, using a central hour and minute hand, a rotating 24-hour ring, and a city ring representing major world cities. Patek Philippe quickly recognized the brilliance of Cottier’s invention and, in 1937, introduced its first world time wristwatch: Ref. 96 HU (“HU” for Heure Universelle ). Over the following decades, Patek Philippe refined the concept with several legendary references. The Ref. 1415 HU of the 1940s and 1950s featured a larger case and improved legibility, while the Ref. 2523 HU of the 1950s is celebrated for its breathtaking cloisonné enamel dials depicting world maps. Today, the Ref. 2523 is considered the holy grail of Patek Philippe World Time watches, with exceptional examples achieving tens of millions at auction. From the 1970s until around 2000, Patek Philippe produced very few World Time watches, until the introduction of Ref. 5110, which marked the beginning of the modern World Time era. This reference remains a favorite here at Bulang & Sons—an icon that perfectly balances technical ingenuity with timeless elegance. b4ed54218ddb: Lanciato nel 1985 in sostituzione del modello ref. 3450, il leggendario «Padellone», il modello ref. 3940 presenta una cassa classica in stile Calatrava con proporzioni e layout del quadrante estremamente puliti. Al suo interno batte il nuovissimo calibro 240 ultra-sottile, il primo movimento Patek Philippe a utilizzare un micro-rotore. Proposto in quattro metalli, oro giallo, oro rosa, oro bianco e platino, il modello è stato prodotto in tre serie con una produzione che è durata fino al 2007. Questo esemplare in oro giallo fa parte della seconda serie che si distingue dalla prima principalmente per i suoi contatori con bordi smussati che danno unimpressione complessiva più ampia. Anche la firma a ore 12 è leggermente più grande e laccento grave di Geneve è scomparso. Il quadrante, con raro calendario italiano, presenta una patina molto omogenea e piacevole. Cinturino in coccodrillo marrone con fibbia Patek Philippe in oro giallo 18k. Lorologio è in ottime condizioni, con estratto degli archivi Patek Philippe che conferma la produzione nel 1989 e un anno di garanzia di negozio sul funzionamento. Spedizioni in tutto il mondo con corriere assicurato FedEx.
856b010e7461: Rarissimo Rolex Daytona Ref. 6241 con quadrante nero Paul Newman. Questo bellissimo orologio prodotto nel 1968, seriale 176XXXX, è in condizioni eccezionali. Si tratta di una rara referenza, 6241, prodotta solo per tre anni, dal 1966 al 1969. Orologio originale e coevo in tutte le sue componenti. Movimento a carica manuale cal. 722-1, revisionato e perfettamente funzionante. Bracciale Oyster rivettato 7205 con terminali 71 e chiusura datata I/68. Il quadrante nero Paul Newman è in ottimo stato di conservazione. A rendere ancora più attrattivo questo esemplare è il corredo che racconta la sua storia! Venne infatti venduto nel febbraio del 1970 dallo storico concessionario Brunati con sede in Bahnhofstrasse 24 a Zurigo a un acquirente di nazionalità Argentina, accompagnato da un libretto di garanzia in lingua spagnola, debitamente compilato e timbrato. I successivi interventi di manutenzione di cui abbiamo traccia grazie allulteriore documentazione cartacea accompagnatoria, ovvero due revisioni eseguite nel 1976 e successivamente nel 1999, presso il concessionario Rolex di Buenos Aires, ci danno prova della lunga appartenenza al primo proprietario. La scatola e contro scatola originali completano questo corredo incredibile! Spedizioni in tutto il mondo con corriere assicurato Fedex.

d242a028312c: Il Seamaster PloProf 600 è stato ideato nel 1967, ma è stato lanciato sul mercato solo nel 1971, rimanendo in produzione fino alla fine degli anni 70. La sua caratteristica cassa monoblocco, progettata per resistere a pressioni idriche estreme, ha reso il PloProf un orologio leggendario tra i collezionisti. Tra le caratteristiche più distintive figurano il meccanismo della corona protetto sui lati e il cursore di sicurezza dai colori vivaci che blocca la lunetta girevole. Queste funzioni erano rivoluzionarie per lepoca e rimangono una testimonianza affascinante della forza innovativa di Omega. Allinterno, è alimentato da un robusto movimento automatico Omega cal.1002, rinomato per la sua durata e precisione. In combinazione con unimpressionante impermeabilità fino a 600 metri da cui il nome “Plongeur Professionnel” questo orologio dimostra in modo impressionante di essere stato progettato per un uso professionale serio. Questo modello appartiene alla prima generazione in cui la profondità era indicata solo in metri; solo in seguito è apparsa la doppia misurazione in metri/piedi. Il quadrante è il Mk2, prodotto nel 1972. È stato utilizzato per lo scopo previsto, motivo per cui è stato sottoposto a manutenzione in fabbrica nel 2010. Il bellissimo bracciale “Mesh” 1266/237 completa questo pezzo di storia. Spedizioni in tutto il mondo con corriere FedEx assicurato.

53d9d03db733: La referenza CK 2998 venne prodotta dal 1959 fino al 1963. Divenne di fatto, il primo Omega nello spazio e inaugurò la serie di esemplari utilizzati per le esplorazioni spaziali. Proprio di questo modello si innamorò Walter Schirra – Wally, per gli amici – pilota della US Navy che acquistò lo Speedmaster CK 2998 in una gioielleria di Houston, qualche mese prima di partire per lo Spazio come pilota titolare della missione Mercury-Atlas 8, lanciata da Cape Canaveral il 3 ottobre 1962, a bordo della capsula Sigma 7. Durante quelle 9 ore e passa di volo, aveva al polso il suo Speedmaster. Lo aveva indossato a titolo personale, con l’intenzione di utilizzarlo come back-up per l’orologio di bordo. Anche se non fu una scelta ufficiale dell’agenzia spaziale, il CK 2998 funzionò perfettamente. Divenne così, di fatto, il primo Omega nello spazio e inaugurò la serie di esemplari utilizzati – poi su protocollo Nasa – per le esplorazioni spaziali. Questo bellissimo esemplare è in particolare una referenza 2998-3, perfettamente coevo in ogni sua componente e caratterizzato da una piacevolissima e calda patina del tempo. Completo della sua scatola originale e del suo tag! Lorologio viene completato da un documento Omega che ne dimostra lesamina fatta in fabbrica nel 2024, lavori poi non effettuati per mantenere loriginal
